cards.jurisdiction: India (SEBI; AMFI)
applies_to: mutual fund distributor posts and websites

rules.rule: An advertisement is 'any communication issued by or on behalf of the mutual fund or asset management company that may influence the investment decision' of an investor (reg 2(c)).

Ads must be 'accurate, true, fair, clear, complete, unambiguous and concise' and consistent with the SID, SAI and KIM; no statements 'based on assumption/projections', no testimonials or 'any ranking based on any criteria', no exaggerated slogans, no unfair comparisons (Fifth Schedule (a)-(h)).
'No celebrities shall form part of the advertisement' (Fifth Schedule (e)).

Standard warning, no words added or removed: 'Mutual Fund investments are subject to market risks, read all scheme related documents carefully.' Vernacular ads carry it in that language; audio-visual ads show and voice it, e.g. 'fourteen (14) words running for at least five (5) seconds' (Fifth Schedule (i)-(k)).

Performance ads: CAGR for at least 1, 3 and 5 years and since inception, point-to-point returns on Rs 10,000, computed to the last month-end; state regular or direct plan; scheme and additional benchmarks; the fund manager's other schemes; 'Where the scheme has been in existence for less than six months, past performance shall not be provided' (Master Circular 14.2).

Specialized Investment Fund ads carry their own fixed warning, which begins 'Investments in Specialized Investment Fund involves relatively higher risk including potential loss of capital, liquidity risk and market volatility.' (Master Circular 21.13.5).

Distributors show 'AMFI-registered Mutual Fund Distributor' with their name and ARN (at least font size 12 in print, legible in all other communication); do 'not provide any indicative portfolio or indicative yield or indicative return'; use AMC marketing material as supplied; may not use 'Adviser' or 'Wealth Manager' in their name unless SEBI-registered.

MFD YouTube and social media: educational content only, no scheme-specific recommendations or performance claims, disclose MFD status and ARN; no lures of rebates, gifts, 'free advise' or 'free portfolio review' (AMFI FAQ Q.8-Q.9).

checks: Does the piece carry the standard warning word for word (in the ad's language), and in video both on screen and in voice-over?
Is it free of celebrities, testimonials, rankings, star ratings and 'No. 1' claims?
Is it free of projections, 'guaranteed', 'assured', 'safe' or target-return language?
If it shows performance, does it use CAGR for 1, 3, 5 years and since inception, Rs 10,000 point-to-point, plan type, benchmarks, and no figures for a scheme under six months old?
Is every statement consistent with the scheme's SID, SAI and KIM and its riskometer?
For a distributor: are name, ARN and 'AMFI-registered Mutual Fund Distributor' shown, is the scheme creative the AMC's own, and is social content educational rather than a scheme recommendation?

cards.name: SEBI advertisement code for Investment Advisers and Research Analysts (Master Circulars of February 6, 2026; first issued by circulars of April 2023)
cards.summary: In force (Master Circulars for Investment Advisers and for Research Analysts, both dated 6 Feb 2026). Every communication by or for a SEBI-registered adviser or research analyst that may influence investment decisions, social posts and messages included, must show the registered name and SEBI registration number, carry the fixed standard warning and disclaimers, and be approved in advance by the supervisory body. It may never promise or imply assured, minimum or target returns or accuracy, use superlatives, unverified past performance, misleading testimonials or the SEBI logo.
use_for: Websites, landing pages and app copy for SEBI-registered investment advisers (RIAs) and research analysts
Social posts, reels, YouTube scripts, Telegram and WhatsApp messages and newsletters by advisers and analysts
Briefing an adviser who wants a creator or agency campaign
avoid: 'Our calls hit 92% accuracy', 'Target 30% in 6 months', 'Earn Rs 50,000 a month from the market': assured, target and accuracy claims are banned outright.
'India's No. 1 SEBI RIA' or 'Top analyst': superlatives are banned; state a factual award from an independent body instead.
A SEBI logo, a 'SEBI approved' badge or 'SEBI certified returns': the logo is barred and registration is no guarantee of performance.
A reel or SMS with no registration number or warning: when space is short, link to the official website that carries all the details.
Client stories like 'I tripled my money with their tips': testimonials must not mislead, and performance claims need PaRRVA verification.
'Free stock tips' that lead into a paid plan: a report or service may be called free only if it is free without condition.

cards.jurisdiction: India (SEBI; supervisory body for IAs and RAs)

rules.rule: Scope: all communications by or on behalf of the IA or RA that may influence investment decisions, including email, text messaging, messaging platforms, 'social media platforms', radio, TV and video (IA Master Circular 10.1(a)).

Show the name as registered with SEBI, registered office address, SEBI registration number, logo or brand name and CIN if any; on SMS, pop-ups or social media without room for these, give a hyperlink to the official website that carries them (10.1(b)(i), (vi)).

Standard warning in at least 10-point font, unchanged: 'Investment in securities market are subject to market risks. Read all the related documents carefully before investing'; in audio-visual ads, e.g. '20 words running for at least 10 seconds'; translated accurately in non-English ads.

Securities shown as examples need 'The securities quoted are for illustration only and are not recommendatory'; ads carry the disclaimer that SEBI registration, enlistment with the supervisory body and NISM certification 'in no way guarantee performance' or assure returns (RA wording names BSE).

Banned: statements 'based on assumptions or projections'; 'Any misleading or deceptive testimonials'; calling a service free unless free without condition; any assured or risk-free return, and no implied 'minimum returns or target return or percentage accuracy' (10.1(c)).

Banned: past performance or risk-return metrics unless verified by the Past Risk and Return Verification Agency (PaRRVA); superlatives such as 'Best', 'No. 1', 'Top Adviser', 'Leading' (factual independent awards allowed); discrediting other intermediaries.

'Advertisements shall not include SEBI Logo'; prior approval from the SEBI-recognised supervisory body; no games or competitions with prizes; no ads while suspended; keep a copy for five years (10.1(c)-(d)).

checks: Does the piece show the SEBI-registered name and registration number, or link to a website page that shows them with the address and disclaimers?
Is the standard warning present word for word, at least 10-point in print, and both shown and voiced in video?
Is it free of assured, minimum, target, accuracy and 'risk-free' claims, stated or implied?
Is it free of superlatives, the SEBI logo, unverified past-performance figures and misleading testimonials?
If securities are named as examples, is the 'illustration only' disclaimer present?
Has the supervisory body approved the ad before publication, and is a copy kept for five years?

cards.name: Surrogate and brand-extension advertising in India (alcohol, tobacco, betting): CCPA 2022 guideline 6, Cable TV Advertising Code brand-extension proviso, ASCI brand-extension qualification criteria and the 2024-2025 advisories
cards.summary: As read 2026-10-13: an ad that uses another product (soda, music, glassware, a 'news' or 'gaming' app) to keep a liquor, tobacco or betting brand in view is a surrogate ad, banned by CCPA guideline 6 and, on TV, by the Cable TV Code. A real brand extension may be advertised only if the ad shows only that product, makes no reference to the banned one and borrows none of its colours, layout or situations; ASCI and the TV code also test whether the extension really sells. Influencers who promote betting, directly or by surrogate, share the liability.
use_for: Briefs, scripts and social copy for brand extensions of liquor or tobacco companies (soda, water, glassware, music, apparel)
Sports, event and IPL-season sponsorship copy
Influencer and creator scripts for gaming, fantasy and 'news' apps
Reviewing a client's campaign for surrogate risk before it airs
avoid: 'Acme Club Soda, for the moments after 9 pm' shot in a bar with amber glasses and the whisky label's colours: every cue points at the liquor. Show the soda being sold and used as soda, in its own design.
Running a brand-extension ad for a product nobody can buy: ASCI treats an extension that fails its turnover and investment tests as 'a surrogate created to advertise a restricted category'.
An ad budget far larger than the extension's sales (ASCI caps it at 200% of sales in years 1 and 2, falling to 30% after year 4).

Creator reels for a 'free fantasy app' or 'sports news app' that is the front of a betting site: the MIB told influencers to refrain from promoting offshore betting, 'including surrogate advertisements', and posts or accounts can be removed.
Assuming 'we only showed the company name' always protects you: the CCPA proviso protects mere use of a shared name only if nothing else in the ad is objectionable.

cards.jurisdiction: India (CCPA under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019; MIB Cable TV rules; ASCI self-regulation)

rules.rule: No surrogate or indirect ad for goods whose advertising is prohibited or restricted, made 'by circumventing such prohibition or restriction and portraying it to be an advertisement for other goods' (CCPA 2022, guideline 6(1); definition 2(h)).
An ad is surrogate if it 'indicates or suggests directly or indirectly' the banned product, or 'uses any brand name, logo, colour, layout and presentation associated with' it (guideline 6(2)).
Proviso: 'mere use of a brand name or company name' shared with a banned product is not surrogate if the ad is not otherwise objectionable under the guidelines.

On TV and cable, a brand-extension ad must depict only the product advertised, make no direct or indirect reference to the prohibited product, carry no 'nuances or phrases promoting prohibited products', and use no associated colours, layout, presentation or typical situations (rule 7(2)(viii)).

TV brand extensions also need a Chartered Accountant's certificate of real distribution and proportionate spend, an MIB finding of genuine brand extension and CBFC certification before telecast (rule 7(2)(viii), second proviso).

ASCI test: the extension is registered (GST, FDA, FSSAI, TM); over two years old, turnover above Rs 5 crore a year nationally or Rs 1 crore per state; newer, one of Rs 20 lakh a month, Rs 10 crore of exclusive fixed assets, long-term supply contracts, or turnover above 10% of the restricted brand's.
ASCI ad-budget cap: not more than 200% of the extension's sales in years 1 and 2, 100% in year 3, 50% in year 4 and 30% after, counting media, celebrity fees and production.
Betting: the CCPA warns that celebrities and influencers promoting online betting are 'equally liable for participating in an illegal activity' (advisory of 06 Mar 2024).

The MIB advised influencers to refrain from promoting offshore betting and gambling, 'including surrogate advertisements'; non-compliance may lead to 'removal or disabling of social media posts or accounts' (21 Mar 2024).

checks: Does the ad show only the product actually being sold, with no bottle, glass, bar, smoke, pack or play-money cue for the banned product?
Is it free of the banned brand's colours, layout, typography, jingles, taglines and typical situations?
Can the client show the extension is on sale at scale (ASCI turnover or investment test) and that ad spend is within the ASCI cap?
For TV, has the advertiser got the CA certificate, the MIB brand-extension clearance and CBFC certification?
Does any creator or celebrity script avoid promoting betting or gambling platforms, directly or through a surrogate app or brand?

cards.name: ICO Age Appropriate Design Code (Children's code): transparency, published terms and community standards, default settings and nudge techniques, with the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 children's higher protection matters duty
cards.summary: The ICO's statutory code (in force since 2 September 2020) for any online service likely to be accessed by children in the UK, not only services made for children. For a writer it governs privacy notices, terms, community standards, consent prompts and settings copy: concise, prominent, age-suited language, bite-sized just-in-time explanations, high-privacy defaults and no nudging. The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 added a children's higher protection matters duty with the same scope (ICO: all its data protection provisions in force as of 19 June 2026).
use_for: Writing privacy notices, terms and community standards for apps, games, edtech, streaming and retail sites that children may use
Writing just-in-time notices at the moment a feature starts using a child's data (location, camera, sharing)
Writing settings, consent and sign-up screens, including age questions
Reviewing button labels and prompts for nudges that steer a child to share more
avoid: One long adult privacy policy and nothing else. Add short, age-suited explanations where the data use happens: 'Turning this on shows your town to friends. Ask a grown-up if you are not sure.'
Promising protections the product does not deliver ('a moderator checks every message'). The code says information must not promise protections or standards that are not routinely upheld.

Nudging copy and design: a big bright 'Yes, share!' beside a tiny grey 'no thanks', or 'Most kids turn this on'. Give both choices equal weight and neutral words ('Share my location' / 'Keep it private').
Pre-selecting an older age band on an age question, or offering no option for the child's true age. Use a neutral, empty age picker.
Settings copy that defaults to sharing or treats lower privacy as the normal choice. Write the high-privacy option as the default and explain what changes if the child switches it.
Assuming the code only matters for children's brands: it covers services 'likely to be accessed by children' such as games, social apps and general retail sites.

cards.jurisdiction: United Kingdom (ICO statutory code under the Data Protection Act 2018; UK GDPR as amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025)

rules.rule: Scope: 'information society services likely to be accessed by children' in the UK, including apps, games, social media, streaming, news, educational and retail sites; 'It is not restricted to services specifically directed at children.'

Privacy information, terms, policies and community standards 'must be concise, prominent, and in clear language suited to the age of the child', with 'bite-sized' explanations when a data use is activated.

Information must not 'promise protections or standards that are not routinely upheld'; legally drafted terms can carry child-friendly explanations alongside; use diagrams, cartoons, video, icons and layered text tailored to age (Standard 4).
'Uphold your own published terms, policies and community standards' (Standard 6).

Settings must be high privacy by default unless there is a compelling reason; optional uses are individually activated by the child, and users should not be nudged towards a lower privacy option (Standard 7).

'Do not use nudge techniques to lead or encourage children to provide unnecessary personal data or turn off privacy protections'; no nudges that might lead children to lie about their age (Standard 13).

Data (Use and Access) Act 2025: services in scope of the code must take the 'children's higher protection matters' into account when designing data protection; conforming to the code is likely to comply (ICO).

cards.penalty: Not conforming to the code means 'you may find it difficult to demonstrate compliance with the law and you may invite regulatory action' (ICO, About this code).
checks: Is every privacy notice, term and community standard short, easy to find and written in words the youngest likely user understands?
Is there a bite-sized explanation at each point where a feature starts using a child's data?
Does the copy avoid promising any safety or privacy protection the service does not routinely deliver?
Are the yes and no options for any data or privacy choice given equal weight and neutral wording?
Is the high-privacy option the default and described as the normal choice?
Does the age question start empty, with the child's true age available?
For an older-child audience, does the copy explain consequences rather than just push a choice?

cards.name: UK Online Safety Act 2023: duties on user-to-user and search services (clear and accessible terms of service, age limits) and the false and threatening communications offences
cards.summary: UK law, regulated by Ofcom, for any service with UK links that lets users post content, plus search services. For a writer it means two things: terms of service and safety policies must be clear, easy to find and written at the reading age of the youngest permitted user, and nobody may send knowingly false messages meant to cause harm or messages that threaten death or serious harm. Offences in force since 31 Jan 2024, illegal content duties since 17 Mar 2025, children's safety duties since 25 Jul 2025.
use_for: Writing or rewriting terms of service, community guidelines and content policies for an app, forum, marketplace or social platform with UK users
Writing the safety, reporting and complaints sections of a help centre
Checking satire, prank, hoax or 'shock' campaign copy that will reach UK audiences
Briefing a product team on what Ofcom expects user-facing policy text to look like
avoid: Terms written for lawyers only. Do not bury the reporting and takedown process in clause 14.3 of a 9,000-word document; give it its own signposted heading and write it at the youngest permitted user's reading age (for a 13+ app: 'If you see something illegal, tap Report. We review reports and remove illegal posts quickly.').

Terms that promise more than the service does. Category 1 services must uphold their terms, and every service must enforce its age limits consistently: do not write 'we check every account's age' unless the product actually does.

Hoax or fake-news style marketing ('BREAKING: the city's water supply is poisoned, buy our filter now'). A message the sender knows is false, sent to cause non-trivial harm, can be the false communications offence. Use clearly signalled fiction or a real, sourced fact instead.

Threat-flavoured copy, even as a joke ('Reply or we'll find you'). A message conveying a threat of death or serious harm, including serious financial loss, can be the threatening communications offence. Write the urgency without the threat.
Assuming a non-UK company is outside the Act. It reaches services with links to the UK; check before telling a client it does not apply.

cards.jurisdiction: United Kingdom (Online Safety Act 2023; Ofcom is the online safety regulator; offences prosecuted under Part 10)

rules.rule: Scope: 'The Act's duties apply to search services and services that allow users to post content online', including services run from outside the UK 'should they have links to the UK' (GOV.UK explainer).

Terms must say how users are protected from illegal content, how reported illegal content is swiftly taken down, what proactive technology is used and how complaints are handled (Ofcom code measure ICU G1).

Those provisions must be easy to find ('clearly signposted for the general public'), laid out to help UK users read them, 'written to a reading age comprehensible for the youngest individual permitted to use the service', and usable with keyboard navigation and screen readers (ICU G3).

Social media companies must 'enforce their age limits consistently' and specify their age-limit measures in the terms of service; Category 1 services must 'uphold their terms of service' (GOV.UK explainer).

False communications offence: sending a message that 'conveys information that the person knows to be false', intended to 'cause non-trivial psychological or physical harm', without reasonable excuse (CPS).

Threatening communications offence: a message that 'conveys a threat of death or serious harm', sent intending or reckless as to fear it will be carried out; serious harm includes 'serious financial loss' (CPS).
Dates: offences 'came into effect on 31 January 2024'; illegal content codes in force 17 March 2025; protection of children codes in force 25 July 2025 (GOV.UK, Ofcom).

checks: Does the policy explain how users are protected from illegal content, how reports are handled and how to complain, under its own clear heading?
Is that section signposted so a visitor who has not signed up can find it?
Is it written at the reading age of the youngest user the service allows without parental consent?
Does every age-limit or safety promise in the copy match what the product actually does?
Is the text usable with a screen reader and keyboard navigation (real headings, no text baked into images)?
Is the piece free of claims the writer knows are false that could cause someone real harm, and of any threat of death, serious injury or serious financial loss, even as a joke?

cards.name: WhatsApp Business Messaging Policy, template categories and the AI Providers clause of the Meta Terms for WhatsApp Business Platform
cards.summary: Meta's rules for every business message on WhatsApp (policy page last updated 23 Sep 2026). Message only people who opted in, honour every opt-out, open conversations only with an approved template used for its own category, reply freely only inside the 24-hour customer service window, give automated chats a human escalation path, never ask for card or ID numbers, and keep restricted goods out. A separate clause bars providers of general-purpose AI assistants from using the Platform when the AI is the main product (in force from 15 Jan 2026 per news coverage).
use_for: Writing WhatsApp marketing, utility and authentication templates for a business
Writing the opt-in line on a checkout, form or ad that collects WhatsApp numbers
Scripting WhatsApp chatbots and auto-replies
Checking whether a client's product or campaign may be messaged on WhatsApp at all
avoid: Messaging a bought or scraped number list. Opt-in must come from the recipient; write an opt-in line that names the message types ('Send me order updates and offers on WhatsApp').

Dressing a promotion as a utility message ('Your order shipped! Plus 20% off your next buy'). Mixed content counts as marketing and Meta can recategorise the template; keep the update clean and send the offer as a marketing template.
Anything but the code in an authentication template: no links, media or emoji, and no upsell.
Bot scripts with no way out. Automated replies need a prompt, clear path to a human, phone, email, web or store support; write 'Type AGENT to talk to a person' into the flow.
Asking customers to type a full card number, bank account number or ID number in chat. Send a secure link to the business's own payment or KYC page instead.
Templates that hide the opt-out or ignore 'STOP'. Every opt-out request, on or off WhatsApp, must be honoured.
Promoting restricted categories (alcohol, tobacco, drugs, medical products, real-money gaming, dating, MLM, payday loans and more) unless the Regulated Vertical rules allow it in that country.
Using the WhatsApp Business Platform for a political party, candidate or campaign: the policy prohibits it.

cards.jurisdiction: Global platform policy (Meta: WhatsApp Business App and WhatsApp Business Platform); applies alongside local law such as India's DPDP Act or UK PECR
applies_to: opt-in lines on forms, checkout and ads

rules.rule: Contact people only if they gave you their number or username and you have 'opt-in permission from the recipient confirming that they wish to receive subsequent messages or calls from you'.
'You must respect all requests (either on or off WhatsApp) by a person to block, discontinue, or otherwise opt out of communications from you'; best practice is separate opt-in per message category.

'You may only initiate conversations using an approved Message Template', used 'only for its designated purpose'; free-form replies only inside 'the 24-hour customer service window, which opens and resets with each user message'.
Automation is allowed in the window but 'must also have available prompt, clear, and direct escalation paths' such as an in-chat human agent, phone, email or web support.
'Don't share or ask people to share full length individual payment card numbers, financial account numbers, personal ID card numbers, or other sensitive identifiers.'

No impersonating another business, no offensive or sexually explicit content, no discrimination, and no promoting listed restricted goods and services except country-limited Regulated Verticals; selling via catalogs follows the Meta Commerce Policy.

Categories: 'Only authentication templates can be used to send a one-time passcode'; utility templates are 'non-promotional'; templates with mixed content 'are also considered marketing' (Meta developer docs).

AI Providers are 'strictly prohibited from accessing or using the WhatsApp Business Platform' to offer AI when it is 'the primary (rather than incidental or ancillary) functionality' (Meta terms, s.4.7).

cards.penalty: If content or actions violate the terms or policies, 'we may limit or remove your access to our services' (WhatsApp Business Messaging Policy); Meta can also pause or reject any template.
checks: Has every recipient opted in to this type of message, and does the opt-in wording name the message types?
Is the template in the right category, with no promotional line inside a utility or authentication template?
Does an authentication template carry only the code and its context, with no link, media or emoji?
Is any free-form reply going out inside 24 hours of the customer's last message?
Does the bot or auto-reply flow show a way to reach a human or other support channel?
Is the copy free of requests for full card, bank account or ID numbers?
Is the product or offer outside the prohibited and restricted list, or allowed as a Regulated Vertical in that country?
Does the message tell people how to stop receiving this category of message?
